beats.narration: A prototype answers one question: does the connection work? A regulated production deployment answers four more. Who is the model acting as, and is that identity auditable? What data can it reach, and where does that data go? Can an administrator lock the configuration? And can every access be logged for a compliance audit? None of these are exotic. They're the same questions any system touching regulated data must answer. The discipline is answering them at design time.

items.text: can an admin LOCK the config?

beats.narration: Authentication follows the service's identity model. Remote service tied to user identity, a SaaS tool, a cloud product? OAuth. The server answers unauthorized, the client opens a browser sign-in, the user approves, and a token is issued and stored. Nobody copies a secret by hand. Remote service with a service identity, like an internal API? An API key, passed through an environment variable, injected at the point of execution. In CI, the pipeline runner supplies it as a secret. And a local service touching the filesystem? No network auth at all: stdio transport, with filesystem permissions and deny rules as the boundary.

elements.text: Auth follows identity

user identity → OAuth
(401 → sign-in → token stored)

service identity → API key
in an env var, injected at runtime
local → stdio + file permissions + deny rules
the best secret is one nobody handles

beats.narration: Keeping the credential safe is its own discipline, built on three practices. Separation: the config file holds a variable name, never the value. Config files get committed and cloned. Values that ride along enter history forever. Placement: a local, short-lived secret lives in an environment variable. A shared or audited one belongs in a secret store, which centralizes the value, logs who reads it, and lets one rotation update every consumer. And rotation: on a schedule, and immediately on any suspected exposure, because an exposed key cannot be made secret again. Two habits make rotation painless: scope each credential to the narrowest access its task needs, and keep a record of who uses it, so rotating doesn't become an outage hunt.

elements.text: Secrets: three practices

① separation — file holds the NAME,
never the value

② placement — env var (local) ·
secret store (shared, audited)
③ rotation — scheduled + on exposure

narrow scope +
known consumers =
painless rotation

beats.narration: The three answers a regulated customer will actually check. Configuration control: enterprise managed settings deploy the auth setup organization-wide, and no individual developer can change it during an audit window. Access logging: a post tool use hook writes every tool call to an audit store. It fires deterministically, on every call. The model can't skip it, and that's precisely why an auditor accepts it. And data residency: an endpoint pinned to a region, on a platform deployment that keeps processing there, turns where does our data go from a shrug into a checkable answer.

elements.text: What the auditor checks
config lock → enterprise managed settings

audit log → PostToolUse hook, every call,
un-skippable by the model
residency → region-pinned endpoint + platform
"where does data go?" — a checkable answer

beats.narration: The watch-out story this time is quietly infuriating, because nothing was broken. An OAuth connection, tested end to end in staging, moved to production... and every sign-in loops back to the login screen with a redirect mismatch. The cause: OAuth redirect URIs are registered per host. The app was registered for staging dot my company dot com. Production wasn't on the list, so the provider rejected every attempt. And the security reviewer's second flag was just as important: most enterprise customers require separate OAuth app registrations per environment. Same app across staging and prod is itself a finding. The fix is procedural: the redirect registration goes on the deployment checklist, so it's done before the cutover, not discovered at the first failed sign-in.

beats.narration: This whole module compresses into three questions you ask before any high-risk agentic work, and code modernization is the perfect example: what's the blast radius if it goes wrong? How is every change audited? And who approves each phase before the next begins? Answer those, and the tools, plan mode, hooks, managed settings, slot themselves in.
